obtained.how: agency copy: the USGS publications warehouse's own PDF of the report (22 PDF pages, text layer); the conversion table read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: the report's cover (PDF p. 1) and contents
bibliography.note: Dudley, Robert W., Olson, Scott A. & Handley, Michael. 1997. A preliminary study of runoff of selected contaminants from rural Maine highways. USGS Water-Resources Investigations Report 97-4041, Augusta, Maine; iv + 18 pp. Prepared with MDOT, MDEP and the University of Maine Water Research Institute.

claims.claim: A Maine gravel road serving summer cottages exported 9.0 kg TP ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹
claims.location: p. 15 (PDF p. 19), Table 10; p. iv (PDF p. 4), conversion factors; p. 1 (PDF p. 5)
claims.conditions: one site, Kimball Pond Road, New Sharon (Franklin County), an unpaved road with 'seasonal traffic serving several residences and a large number of summer cottages'; September 1992–August 1993; TP by persulfate digestion (all forms, which the authors call 'a maximum total phosphorus loading'); loads per area of the site's 13,200-ft² drainage (the west half of the road, its ditch and a 4–6-ft berm)
claims.note: 8 lb/acre/yr × 1.12 (the report's factor) = 8.96 kg/ha/yr. The same table shows the two paved highways exported more TP per area (22 and 33 lb/acre/yr); the gravel road's distinction was the highest biologically available P (1.7–2 vs 0.9–1.3 lb/acre/yr). The paper's lead-in 'Gravel camp roads are among the most intense sources per hectare' should rest on that available P, not on TP

claims.quote: correction factor of 21.6 percent for the KPR site
claims.conditions: NaOH-extractable ('biologically-available') P as a share of persulfate TP in KPR road sediment samples (Table 9), applied to the TP load; the alternative regression estimate gave 2 lb/acre/yr available (25 % of TP)

claims.claim: together with 41 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ of sediment
claims.quote: total sediment loads ranged from 36,500 to 148,000 lb/acre
claims.conditions: KPR is the 36,500 lb/acre/yr end (the paved sites 121,000 and 148,000); 'total sediment' includes particles up to 1–2 mm

claims.claim: gravel roads yield 9.0 kg TP per hectare of road a year, 21.6 % available, applied to a 4.5-m road surface
claims.source_value: 9.0 kg TP per hectare of the site's DRAINAGE AREA: the western half of the roadway plus the ditch along it and a 4–6-ft-high berm (13,200 ft², with 400 ft of the ditch lined), not per hectare of road surface
claims.location: p. 2 (PDF p. 6), site descriptions; p. 3 (PDF p. 7)
claims.quote: drainage area is 13,200 ft2 and consists of the western half of the roadway
claims.conditions: as above; the report gives no road length or width for the site
claims.note: applying the yield to the road surface alone (ROAD_W 4.5 m) uses a smaller area than the one it was measured on. If the 400 ft of lined ditch spans the whole catchment (the report does not say), the drainage strip is ~10 m wide for half a road, and the per-metre-of-road load would be roughly four times the model's [inf]

claims.claim: Maine DEP's 2.0 kg/ha available P for roads
claims.quote: recommends an adjustment coefficient of 0.5 yielding 3.5 x 0.5 = 1.75 lb/acre/yr
claims.conditions: MDOT's TP export value of 3.5 lb/acre/yr for road-surface runoff (from Driscoll et al. 1990's mostly urban interstate data) times MDEP's availability coefficient 0.5 (Noel, Dennis, Dennis & Kuhns 1992)
claims.note: 1.75 lb/acre/yr × 1.12 = 1.96 kg/ha/yr ≈ 2.0; strictly MDOT's export value with MDEP's coefficient

claims.conditions: Route 2 (ADT 6,540; repaved during the study) and Route 27 (ADT 1,690); winter sand plowed over the guard rails, so the paved sites' loads are 'likely to be low'

notes: Caveats the report itself lists (p. 16): one year of data; many runoff events unsampled or partly sampled; snow from outside the KPR catchment piled in its ditch; persulfate TP overstates algal-available P. Dissolved orthophosphate at KPR was only 0.04 lb/acre/yr.
